# GRPC deadline rules

Detailed entries for `GRPC-007..GRPC-008`. Each follows the four-part
**What / Why / How / When NOT to apply** shape.

---

## GRPC-007 — Clients set a deadline on every RPC

**What.** Every gRPC call runs under a deadline. Derive a timed context from
the caller's context and pass it to the call:

```go
ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 2*time.Second)
defer cancel()
resp, err := client.GetUser(ctx, req)
```

The deadline propagates to the server over the wire (`grpc-timeout` header);
the server then enforces the remaining budget. The same ctx bounds streaming
clients.

**Why.** Without a deadline, a hung peer leaves the call blocked indefinitely —
the caller's goroutine and connection never unwind, and the caller's own
callers wait behind it. In a chain of three services each blocking on the next
with no deadline, one slow leaf blocks N goroutines × requests across the
whole path — latency tails, goroutine leaks, and cascading timeouts. This is
the most common production gRPC failure mode, and setting a deadline is the
primary defense.

**How.**

```go
ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(parentCtx, 2*time.Second)
defer cancel()
resp, err := client.GetUser(ctx, req)
if errors.Is(err, context.DeadlineExceeded) {
    // call exceeded its budget — return or retry per your policy
    return nil, status.FromContextError(err).Err()
}
```

grpc-go maps `context.DeadlineExceeded` to `codes.DeadlineExceeded`
automatically.

**When NOT to apply.** Fire-and-forget or intentionally long-lived calls want a
very long deadline rather than none — an ID-less reconnect hang is the failure
you're guarding against. Long-poll/SSE-style APIs: keep a generous but finite
deadline per chunk. In all cases prefer *some* budget over zero.

---

## GRPC-008 — Handlers honor the context: check `ctx.Err()`, propagate downstream

**What.** A handler treats the incoming ctx as its deadline budget: check
`ctx.Err()` in loops and blocking waits, propagate ctx into every downstream
call (database, HTTP, another RPC), and return promptly when it fires. grpc-go
converts `context.DeadlineExceeded`/`context.Canceled` into the canonical codes
automatically when you return the context error.

**Why.** The server received a *remaining* budget; a handler that ignores it
keeps consuming CPU, database connections, and downstream RPCs after the caller
already gave up — "zombie requests" that turn deadline timeouts into resource
exhaustion. Honoring ctx is what makes client deadline propagation (GRPC-007)
stop work end-to-end instead of just making the caller wait.

**How.**

```go
func (s *svc) Drain(ctx context.Context, req *pb.DrainRequest) (*pb.Empty, error) {
    for {
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            return nil, ctx.Err()   // grpc-go maps to DeadlineExceeded/Canceled
        case batch := <-s.jobs:
            if err := insert(ctx, batch); err != nil {
                return nil, err
            }
        }
    }
}
```

Downstream calls get the same ctx, or one derived with a **shorter** remaining
budget — never longer — e.g. `context.WithTimeout(ctx, 500*time.Millisecond)`.

**When NOT to apply.** Cleanup that must finish after the deadline (flush a
buffer, close a handle) runs in a fresh scoped context with its own short
timeout, not the request ctx — see GO-006/GO-008 for how to bound that without
leaking.

## GRPC-023 — Retry through a per-method `retryPolicy` in the service config, with codes that are safe for that method

**What.** Configure client retries in the gRPC service config, per method:
`methodConfig[].retryPolicy` with `maxAttempts`, `initialBackoff`,
`maxBackoff`, `backoffMultiplier` and `retryableStatusCodes`. `UNAVAILABLE`
is the usual code. Add others (`ABORTED`, `INTERNAL`) only for methods
that are safe to run twice. Don't wrap stubs in hand-written retry loops.

**Why.** Without a policy, gRPC retries only "transparently": when it is
certain the server never processed the RPC. So a backend restart reaches
every caller as `UNAVAILABLE`. In a run against a server that failed its
first two calls with `UNAVAILABLE`, the call returned `Unavailable` after 1
attempt with no policy, and `OK` after 3 with the policy below. Which
codes are safe is your decision: "gRPC retries do not provide a mechanism
to specifically mark a method as idempotent" (gRFC A6). A retried
non-idempotent method (a charge, a create) can apply twice when the first
attempt failed after the server acted. A hand-written loop also misses
what the built-in retry does: exponential backoff with ±20% jitter,
`retryThrottling`, server pushback, and no retries after the RPC is
committed ("Once the response header is received, the RPC is committed").

**How.**

```go
const serviceConfig = `{
  "methodConfig": [{
    "name": [{"service": "items.v1.ItemService", "method": "GetItem"}],
    "retryPolicy": {
      "maxAttempts": 4,
      "initialBackoff": "0.1s",
      "maxBackoff": "1s",
      "backoffMultiplier": 2,
      "retryableStatusCodes": ["UNAVAILABLE"]
    }
  }]
}`

conn, err := grpc.NewClient(target,
    grpc.WithTransportCredentials(creds),
    grpc.WithDefaultServiceConfig(serviceConfig))
```

`WithDefaultServiceConfig` applies only when the name resolver supplies
no valid service config. One published through DNS or xDS replaces it.

**When NOT to apply.** Methods with side effects and no idempotency key
stay out of the policy, or list only codes that mean the request was not
processed. Retries add load during an outage, so high-fan-in clients
should also set `retryThrottling`. Clients cap `maxAttempts` at 5 ("Values
greater than 5 are treated as 5"). The deadline covers all attempts
("gRPC's call deadline applies across all attempts"), so retries never
extend GRPC-007's budget.

## GRPC-026 — Set wait-for-ready on calls that should outlast a backend restart, always under a deadline

**What.** For RPCs that should wait for a backend instead of failing
fast (batch jobs, calls at client startup, internal service-to-service
traffic), set wait-for-ready: `grpc.WaitForReady(true)` per call in
grpc-go, or `"waitForReady": true` in the method config. Always pair it
with a deadline (GRPC-007).

**Why.** By default, an RPC sent while the channel is in
`TRANSIENT_FAILURE` (every address failed to connect) "will fail
immediately", so a few seconds of rollout turn into `UNAVAILABLE` errors.
With wait-for-ready the RPC queues until the channel is `READY` or its
deadline passes. In a run: `Unavailable` without it; `OK` with it, once
the server came up 0.5 s later; and `DeadlineExceeded` against an
address that never came up, with a 200 ms deadline. The deadline is what
bounds the wait.

**How.**

```go
ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 5*time.Second)
defer cancel()
resp, err := client.GetItem(ctx, req, grpc.WaitForReady(true))
```

**When NOT to apply.** User-facing calls that should fail fast and fall
back (a cache, a degraded response): with wait-for-ready they spend the
whole deadline waiting. Without a deadline, a backend that never returns
blocks the call forever. It only covers connection state. An RPC that
reaches the server and fails still fails (GRPC-023 covers retries).
